what: Floor & Decor sells hard-surface flooring - tile, wood, laminate, vinyl and natural stone - plus installation materials, from very large warehouse-format stores. It buys direct from factories around the world and keeps deep stock on the floor, so a contractor can walk out with enough tile for a whole job the same day.
customers: Professional installers and contractors, who make up a large share of sales, and homeowners doing remodels. Demand follows home sales and renovation spending.
money: Tile, wood, laminate, vinyl and stone, sold from warehouse stores at low everyday prices.
Setting materials, tools, vanities and decorative items that go with a flooring job.
moat: Scale in sourcing and inventory depth. Buying direct from mills and holding thousands of products in stock lets Floor & Decor undercut specialty flooring shops on price and beat home centres on selection.
risks: Existing-home sales remain depressed, and flooring is one of the first projects people defer when they are not moving.
The store-opening plan needs capital, and new stores dilute margins until they mature.
Tariffs on imported tile and flooring raise costs for a model built on direct global sourcing.
opportunities: At about 21 times earnings and 1.0 times sales, the shares price in a far slower future than the business delivered before the housing slowdown.
Every year of deferred remodelling builds pent-up demand that returns when housing turnover recovers.
watch: Comparable-store sales. Revenue has barely moved from $4.4 billion in 2023 to $4.7 billion over the last twelve months, which means new stores are carrying the growth while existing ones go backwards.
view: Floor & Decor was one of the great retail growth stories of the last decade, and the share price is now about $47, valuing the company at $4.9 billion. The business has not broken: it still sells more flooring per store than anyone, and it still earns $240 million a year after tax. What happened is that its revenue stalled at around $4.5 billion for three years as American home sales fell to their lowest level in a generation, and a stock priced for 20% growth was repriced for none.

The question that decides the investment is whether the stalled comparable sales are cyclical or structural. Cyclical is the more likely answer. People replace floors when they buy a house or prepare to sell one, and existing-home turnover is far below normal because owners are locked into cheap mortgages. That does not last for ever. The structural worry - that home centres and online sellers have caught up on selection - is real at the edges but does not show in the gross margin, which is where losing pricing power would appear first.

At 21 times earnings and 14 times free cash flow, the shares are no longer expensive for a business with this record, but they are not a bargain either while earnings are depressed and the store-opening plan absorbs cash. I would treat this as a housing-recovery option with a good operator attached. Buying now means accepting that the wait could be another year or two; the reward for patience is a company whose earnings could rise sharply on the same store base once turnover returns.
bull: Housing turnover recovers, comparable sales turn positive, and margins on a larger store base lift earnings well above the current $240 million.
bear: Home sales stay frozen and tariffs squeeze the direct-sourcing advantage, so the stores keep opening into flat demand and returns on new capital fall.
